626.t: Old band music: New Orleans Jazz and other parts handed over
626.s: Looking through his band music, they find New Orleans Jazz and other parts; he gives a piece to the interviewer.
626.q: Yeah, yeah, yeah. Can I see what pieces they played there? I didn't know this was any of it, see. That might have been some of the music, see.

626.t: Bugle-call booklet, signing the music, and his address
626.s: They talk about a bugle-call booklet, he signs his name on the music, gives his address, and agrees to let the interviewer look at the record book.
626.q: Well, that was just as long as the beginners or something. Or anyone on there would like to learn the bugle calls or something. Yes, such as the. You know, to help them in the army or something. Yes. I just, I just put that aside in here.

639.t: Moose Zanko asks where to buy the Bix book
639.s: Zanko asks about 'Bugles for Beiderbecke' after hearing 'My Melancholy Baby'; Allen suggests a London shop.
639.q: Well, I could get the name and address of a place in London. I probably could order it out of Doug Doble's record shop there. I think that's 77 Charing Cross Road, London, England. But I could give you an exact address if you'll call me tomorrow at Tulane. Call you at Tulane? Yes. I sure will. Hi,…

639.t: Caller with old records is sent to Allen at the Tulane jazz archives
639.s: A caller asks if Clyde McCoy is jazz and about her old records; Wiggs gives his view of the word jazz and praises Allen.
639.q: Well, I tell you, I hate to call anything jazz anymore, because everything south of Beethoven has been called jazz, and I don't know what jazz is and what jazz isn't. I know the kind of musicians that I like to play with, and they call that jazz, and that's the best I can do with that.

78.t: Where his 78s and original arrangements are kept
78.s: Horace's sister keeps some 78s in Georgia, 500 more are with friends in Minneapolis, and he has original arrangements in his basement.
78.ch: Touring, recording and Fletcher's band in the 1940s
78.q: She takes things. Very good care of them. Plus I left 500 78's with very good friends of ours in Minneapolis, Minnesota, which we intend this summer, the first week we're off, take off. We're gonna go and get those.

78.t: His sister keeps Fletcher's papers and records in Georgia; cataloguing plan
78.s: After Fletcher and his wife died, the 139th Street house was sold and papers and experimental discs were moved to Horace's sister in Georgia. The interviewer offers to help catalogue them.
78.ch: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
78.q: : Yes, I probably did that sometimes because a lot of times you would try to remember not to repeat, you know, certain things, you know, and it was essential that I did do that. You know, I've got a lot of that stuff, Tom, at my sister's home in Georgia now, you know, because when Fletcher passed…

32.t: Library of music and corrections to a published story about White
32.s: After a tape break the talk turns to his music library and errors in an earlier article, such as being a night watchman or jailed.
32.ch: Corrections and views on early Black music
32.q: I'd like for you to go downstairs and see my wonderful library down there. I think really I've got a library of music down there that's creditable. We do want to go down. See how much I've got anyhow. You couldn't appraise it. I can't appraise it myself.

83.s: Matassa has only old appointment books and Disc Masters logs in storage; sessions were often logged just by label or bandleader, and he was not organized.
83.q: No. The only log I've got, I've got some of my old appointment books, and I've got the master logs from when I was doing Disc Masters.

632.s: Steinau lists the magazines, books, musicians' cards and Esquire jazz books he kept.
632.q: I've got, oh, probably 15 or 20, uh, business cards of various musicians and bands going back, oh, quite a long while. Uh, I've got a Jolly Roll Martin card or two, whether or not it's, whether or not they are original or not, I have no idea. I suspect the reproductions, but I have no way to find…

843.t: The Tulane collection project: interviews and records
843.s: Russell describes collecting interviews with musicians, wives and listeners, and phonograph records.
843.q: Well, it's strictly a collection project at present. We're collecting interviews, trying to preserve all that history of the old. The older the musicians, the better, of course, and other people, too, that happen to hear the music or maybe help promote it. In some cases, the wives and the…

196.t: Piron at Pythian Temple and the Tulane collection
196.s: They discuss the 1920 sheet music and a recording, and Leclerc admires the archive's collection including Sam Rosenbaum's manuscripts.
196.q: Yeah, Piron was a very nice fellow. Yes. Right. At the Pythian Temple, see that? Yeah, Pythian Temple, I see that.

504.s: He has an archive organized by his wife and assistant in several tape formats.
504.q: Yeah as a matter of fact I have an archive, my wife and my assistant Joan Clancy spent quite a lot of time organizing for me. But you know I recorded in different formats: cassettes, DATs, reel-to-reel. Anyway you were going to ask me about favorite albums?

422.t: Donations of 78s and LPs to the Institute
422.s: People constantly offer record collections the Institute has no space for.
422.ch: Rutgers and the Institute of Jazz Studies
422.q: Oh God we get that almost every day. So, but it’s, “Oh my father just died,” or, you know, “he had a collection of 78s.” Mostly it’s LPs that they want to give us. And you

423.t: Plans for the Hamilton archive and liner notes
423.s: Monk describes plans to open the archive and put samples online; both enjoy reading liner notes.
423.q: Oh yeah I always like to read the liner notes, in fact I was always disappointed they didn’t have good liner notes or extensive liner notes.

61.s: He regrets discarding letters from Armstrong and daily calendars.
61.ch: Yale, Stearns and the big bands
61.q: No, I didn’t. I wish I had. In fact, when I left – well, all through my working life, I didn’t keep my daily calendars and all that. I used to, but it just piled up. I had so much paper. And of course I don’t want to put the onus on my wife, but she was right. “Don’t save so much, because it’s…

144.t: Memorabilia: gold 'Blue Train' record and 5,000 tapes
144.s: Fuller describes his archive, the gold record, tapes and his daughter wanting his papers.
144.q: Yes, Like I told you I opened the door one day and is For FedEx brought this great big thing. This thing I could fill up the whole thing there where the fire places. It was a gold record for “Blue Train.” (Laughs) they didn’t know what to do with it so they gave it to me. It is only one left they…

651.t: His archive of letters, videos and photographs
651.s: Letters from famous people, cassettes and photographs that need a jazz-literate archivist and open access.
651.q: Now, this... Turn your camera over here, if you would. This area down here, folks, all of this here, which is really thick, is stuff from... A lot of times it’s famous people. And Lee Konitz’s letters are down in here. I’ve been threatening to pull all this out, and go through it. But it’s going to…

614.s: He keeps only odds and ends at home; a friend has nearly all his recordings, many from bootleg sources.
614.q: And he's still picking up stuff. He finds it everywhere in the world, you know. Through bootleg operations. (Inaudible.)

18.s: The interviewers ask to borrow three of his records to put on tape; he praises one with Cookie Williams and Rex Stewart.
18.ch: Family, Margaret's story and Eutris's memories
18.q: Sure... When it comes to music, she ain't got nothing to do with it. That's music. She don't make no records. I make them.

388.t: Offers to donate papers to the University of Wyoming and the Smithsonian
388.s: Leeman says the University of Wyoming asked for his memorabilia and that he would like important items to go to the Smithsonian.
388.q: Milt, the University of Wyoming wrote me in great length and asked me if they could have any of my papers, drums, pictures or memorabilia -- I can't pronounce that one -- for their archives, and their music department and if I would leave some of them on my demise, and so I wrote them and told them…

98.t: An archive for his DeLisa music
98.s: DeMichael mentions the Institute's archive; Saunders would go through his DeLisa music book with someone and donate items.
98.ch: Pianists, Basie, Lil Armstrong and closing
98.q: Well, that would be beautiful. Well, those things, I would only too happy to, because, like, the Institute and the museum -- what do call it, the New Orleans --

13.t: Lost photographs and scores; end of interview
13.q: Never was a collector. Just like I say, I never figured, you know. Then in the moving, and the separating, and the moving going on, I lost a lot of stuff. That's the way I lost my scores.
